{{Short description|Complex number whose mapping on a coordinate plane produces a triangular lattice}}
{{redirect2|Eulerian integer|Euler integer||List of topics named after Leonhard Euler#Euler's numbers}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Eisenstein integers''' (named after [[Gotthold Eisenstein]]), occasionally also known<ref name="euler-name" /> as '''Eulerian integers''' (after [[Leonhard Euler]]), are the [[complex number]]s of the form
: <math>z = a + b\omega ,</math>
where {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} are [[integer]]s and
: <math>\omega = \frac{-1 + i\sqrt 3}{2} = e^{i2\pi/3}</math>
is a [[Root of unity#General definition|primitive]] (hence non-real) [[cube root of unity]].

[[File:Eisenstein integer lattice.png|thumb|191px|Eisenstein integers as the points of a certain triangular lattice in the complex plane]]
The Eisenstein integers form a [[triangular lattice]] in the [[complex plane]], in contrast with the [[Gaussian integers]], which form a [[square lattice]] in the complex plane. The Eisenstein integers are a [[Countable set|countably infinite set]].

== Properties ==
The Eisenstein integers form a [[commutative ring]] {{math|'''Z'''[''ω'']}} of [[algebraic integer]]s in the [[algebraic number field]] {{math|'''Q'''(''ω'')}} – the third [[cyclotomic field]]. To see that the Eisenstein integers are algebraic integers note that each {{math|1=''z'' = ''a'' + ''bω''}} is a root of the [[monic polynomial]]
: <math>z^2 - (2a - b)\;\!z + \left(a^2 - ab + b^2\right)~.</math>
In particular, {{math|''ω''}} satisfies the equation
: <math>\omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0~.</math>

The product of two Eisenstein integers {{math|''a'' + ''bω''}} and {{mvar|''c'' + ''dω''}} is given explicitly by
: <math>(a + b\;\!\omega) \;\! (c + d\;\!\omega)=(ac - bd) + (bc + ad - bd)\;\!\omega~.</math>

The 2-norm of an Eisenstein integer is just its [[squared modulus]], and is given by
: <math>{\left|a + b\;\!\omega\right|}^2 \,= \, {(a - \tfrac{1}{2} b)}^2 + \tfrac{3}{4} b^2 \, = \, a^2 - ab + b^2~,</math>
which is clearly a positive ordinary (rational) integer.

Also, the [[complex conjugation|complex conjugate]] of {{math|''ω''}} satisfies
: <math>\bar\omega = \omega^2~.</math>

The [[group of units]] in this ring is the [[cyclic group]] formed by the sixth [[roots of unity]] in the complex plane: {{math|{{mset|±1, ±''ω'', ±''ω''<sup>2</sup>}}}}, the Eisenstein integers of norm&nbsp;{{math|1}}.

== Euclidean domain ==
The ring of Eisenstein integers forms a [[Euclidean domain]] whose norm {{math|''N''}} is given by the square modulus, as above:
: <math>N(a+b\,\omega) = a^2 - a b + b^2. </math>

A [[division algorithm]], applied to any dividend {{math|''α''}} and divisor {{math|''β'' ≠ 0}}, gives a quotient {{math|''κ''}} and a remainder {{math|''ρ''}} smaller than the divisor, satisfying:
: <math>\alpha = \kappa \beta +\rho \ \ \text{  with  }\ \ N(\rho) < N(\beta).</math>

Here, {{math|''α''}}, {{math|''β''}}, {{math|''κ''}}, {{math|''ρ''}} are all Eisenstein integers. This algorithm implies the [[Euclidean algorithm]], which proves [[Euclid's lemma]] and the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic|unique factorization]] of Eisenstein integers into Eisenstein primes.

One division algorithm is as follows.  First perform the division in the field of complex numbers, and write the quotient in terms of {{math|''ω''}}:
: <math> \frac{\alpha}{\beta}\ =\ \tfrac{1}{\ |\beta|^2}\alpha\overline{\beta} \ =\ a+bi \ =\  a+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}b+\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}b\omega,</math>
for rational {{math|''a'', ''b'' ∈ '''Q'''}}. Then obtain the Eisenstein integer quotient by rounding the rational coefficients to the nearest integer:
: <math>\kappa = \left\lfloor a+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}b\right\rceil + \left\lfloor \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}b\right\rceil\omega \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \rho = {\alpha} - \kappa\beta.</math>
Here <math>\lfloor x\rceil</math> may denote any of the standard [[rounding]]-to-integer functions.

The reason this satisfies {{math|''N''(''ρ'') < ''N''(''β'')}}, while the analogous procedure fails for most other [[quadratic integer]] rings, is as follows. A [[fundamental domain]] for the ideal {{math|1='''Z'''[''ω'']''β'' = '''Z'''''β'' + '''Z'''''ωβ''}}, acting by translations on the complex plane, is the 60°–120° rhombus with vertices {{math|0}}, {{math|''β''}}, {{math|''ωβ''}}, {{math|''β'' + ''ωβ''}}. Any Eisenstein integer {{math|''α''}} lies inside one of the translates of this [[parallelogram]], and the quotient {{math|''κ''}} is one of its vertices. The remainder is the square distance from {{math|''α''}} to this vertex, but the maximum possible distance in our algorithm is only <math>\tfrac{\sqrt3}2 |\beta|</math>, so <math>|\rho| \leq \tfrac{\sqrt3}2 |\beta|< |\beta|</math>. (The size of {{math|''ρ''}} could be slightly decreased by taking {{math|''κ''}} to be the closest corner.)

== Eisenstein primes ==
{{for|the unrelated concept of an Eisenstein prime of a modular curve|Eisenstein ideal}}

[[File:EisensteinPrimes-01.svg|right|thumb|upright=1.5|Small Eisenstein primes. Those on the green axes are associate to a natural prime of the form {{math|3''n'' + 2}}. All others have an absolute value equal to 3 or square root of a natural prime of the form {{math|3''n'' + 1}}.]]
[[File:Eisenstein primes.svg|right|thumb|upright=1.5|Eisenstein primes in a larger range]]

If {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} are Eisenstein integers, we say that {{math|''x''}} divides {{math|''y''}} if there is some Eisenstein integer {{math|''z''}} such that {{math|1=''y'' = ''zx''}}. A non-unit Eisenstein integer {{math|''x''}} is said to be an Eisenstein prime if its only non-unit divisors are of the form {{math|''ux''}}, where {{math|''u''}} is any of the six units. They are the corresponding concept to the [[Gaussian prime]]s in the Gaussian integers.

There are two types of Eisenstein prime.
* an ordinary [[prime number]] (or ''rational prime'') which is congruent to {{math|2 mod 3}} is also an Eisenstein prime.
* {{math|3}} and each rational prime congruent to {{math|1 mod 3}} are equal to the norm {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> − ''xy'' + ''y''<sup>2</sup>}} of an Eisenstein integer {{math|''x'' + ''ωy''}}. Thus, such a prime may be factored as {{math|(''x'' + ''ωy'')(''x'' + ''ω''<sup>2</sup>''y'')}}, and these factors are Eisenstein primes: they are precisely the Eisenstein integers whose norm is a rational prime.

In the second type, factors of {{math|3}}, <math>1-\omega</math> and <math>1-\omega^2</math> are [[Associate (ring theory)|associates]]: <math>1-\omega=(-\omega)(1-\omega^2)</math>, so it is regarded as a special type in some books.<ref>{{MathWorld|EisensteinPrime}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Primes of the Form x2+ny2: Fermat, Class Field Theory and Complex Multiplication |last=Cox |first=David A. |date=1997-05-08 |isbn=0-471-19079-9 |pages=77 |publisher=Wiley |url=https://www.math.utoronto.ca/~ila/Cox-Primes_of_the_form_x2+ny2.pdf}}</ref>

The first few Eisenstein primes of the form {{math|3''n'' − 1}} are:
: [[2 (number)|2]], [[5 (number)|5]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[23 (number)|23]], [[29 (number)|29]], [[41 (number)|41]], [[47 (number)|47]], [[53 (number)|53]], [[59 (number)|59]], [[71 (number)|71]], [[83 (number)|83]], [[89 (number)|89]], [[101 (number)|101]], ... {{OEIS|id=A003627}}.

Natural primes that are congruent to {{math|0}} or {{math|1}} modulo {{math|3}} are ''not'' Eisenstein primes:<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4242234/x2-x-1-is-reducible-in-mathbbf-p-x-iff-p-equiv-1-mod-3 |title=<math>X^2 +X +1</math> is reducible in <math>\mathbb{F}_p [X]</math> iff <math>p\equiv 1\pmod 3</math>}}</ref> they admit nontrivial factorizations in {{math|'''Z'''[''ω'']}}. For example:
: {{math|3 {{=}} −(1 + 2''ω'')<sup>2</sup>}}
: {{math|7 {{=}} (3 + ''ω'')(2 − ''ω'')}}.

In general, if a natural prime {{math|''p''}} is {{math|1}} modulo {{math|3}} and can therefore be written as {{math|''p'' {{=}} ''a''<sup>2</sup> − ''ab'' + ''b''<sup>2</sup>}}, then it factorizes over {{math|'''Z'''[''ω'']}} as
: {{math|p {{=}} (''a'' + ''bω'')((''a'' − ''b'') − ''bω'')}}.

Some non-real Eisenstein primes are
: {{math|2 + ''ω''}}, {{math|3 + ''ω''}}, {{math|4 + ''ω''}}, {{math|5 + 2''ω''}}, {{math|6 + ''ω''}}, {{math|7 + ''ω''}}, {{math|7 + 3''ω''}}.

Up to conjugacy and unit multiples, the primes listed above, together with {{math|2}} and {{math|5}}, are all the Eisenstein primes of [[absolute value]] not exceeding {{math|7}}.

{{As of|2023|10}}, the largest known real Eisenstein prime is the [[Largest known prime number|12th-largest known prime]] {{math|10223 × 2<sup>31172165</sup> + 1}}, discovered by Péter Szabolcs and [[PrimeGrid]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Largest Known Primes |url=https://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=3 |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=The [[Prime Pages]]}}</ref>

== Eisenstein series ==
The sum of the reciprocals of all Eisenstein integers excluding {{math|0}} raised to the fourth power is {{math|0}}:<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1231810/what-are-the-zeros-of-the-j-function |title=What are the zeros of the j-function?}}</ref>
<math display="block">\sum_{z\in\mathbf{E}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{1}{z^4}=G_4\left(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\right)=0</math>
so <math>e^{2\pi i/3}</math> is a root of [[j-invariant]].
In general <math>G_k\left(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\right)=0</math> if and only if <math>k\not\equiv 0 \pmod 6</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2044686/show-that-g-4i-neq-0-and-g-6-rho-neq-0-rho-e2-pi-i-3 |title=Show that <math>G_4(i)\neq 0</math>, and <math>G_6(\rho)\neq 0</math>, <math>\rho=e^{2\pi i /3}</math>}}</ref>

The sum of the reciprocals of all Eisenstein integers excluding {{math|0}} raised to the sixth power can be expressed in terms of the [[gamma function]]:
<math display="block">\sum_{z\in\mathbf{E}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{1}{z^6}=G_6\left(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}\right)=\frac{\Gamma (1/3)^{18}}{8960\pi^6} \approx 5.86303</math>
where {{math|'''E'''}} are the Eisenstein integers and {{math|''G''<sub>6</sub>}} is the [[Eisenstein series]] of weight 6.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Entry 0fda1b – Fungrim: The Mathematical Functions Grimoire |url=https://fungrim.org/entry/0fda1b/ |access-date=2023-06-22 |website=fungrim.org}}</ref>

== Quotient of {{math|'''C'''}} by the Eisenstein integers ==
The [[Quotient ring|quotient]] of the complex plane {{math|'''C'''}} by the [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] containing all Eisenstein integers is a [[complex torus]] of real dimension&nbsp;{{math|2}}. This is one of two tori with maximal [[symmetry]] among all such complex tori.<ref>{{Cite web |title=18.783 Elliptic Curves Lecture 18 |url=https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.783/2022/LectureSlides18.pdf |website=MIT Mathematics |page=8 |quote=To define a complex structure of <math>X(1)</math> we can restrict attention to <math>\mathcal{F}^*</math>. There are three points that complicate matters: <math>i, \rho:=e^{2 \pi i / 3}, \infty</math>.  Lemma Let <math>G_\tau</math> be the stabilizer of <math>\tau \in \mathcal{F}^*</math> in <math>\Gamma</math>. Let <math>S=\left(\begin{array}{cc}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{array}\right)</math> and <math>T=\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right)</math>. Then  <math> G_\tau= \begin{cases}\{ \pm I\} \simeq \mathbb{Z} / 2 \mathbb{Z} & \text { if } \tau \notin\{i, \rho, \infty\} \\ \langle S\rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z} / 4 \mathbb{Z} & \text { if } \tau=i ; \\ \langle S T\rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z} / 6 \mathbb{Z} & \text { if } \tau=\rho \\ \langle \pm T\rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z} & \text { if } \tau=\infty\end{cases} </math>}}</ref> This torus can be obtained by identifying each of the three pairs of opposite edges of a regular hexagon.
[[File:Wrapped hexagon topology.png|thumb|center|Identifying each of the three pairs of opposite edges of a regular hexagon.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Shape of Space |last=Weeks |first=Jeffrey |publisher=CRC Press |year=2001 |pages=115 |author-link=Jeffrey Weeks (mathematician) |quote=Figure 7.13 To physically glue together opposite edges of a hexagon, you must deform the hexagon into the shape of a doughnut surface. A hexagon with abstractly glued edges therefore has the same global topology as a torus.}}</ref>]]
The other maximally symmetric torus is the quotient of the complex plane by the additive lattice of [[Gaussian integers]], and can be obtained by identifying each of the two pairs of opposite sides of a square fundamental domain, such as {{math|[0, 1] × [0, 1]}}.
